summary: This unit teaches you to build and keep effective working relationships as a team leader or manager. You will learn how to earn trust, communicate and consult, apply workplace standards fairly, build networks, prevent and resolve conflict, support people with personal difficulties, handle bullying and harassment reports, and use survey and staffing figures to improve relationships.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It teaches you to build and keep **effective working relationships** with your team, your own manager, other departments, suppliers and customers, and to handle the problems that arise between people: conflict, poor performance, personal difficulties, bullying and harassment.

A supervisor's results come through other people. Good relationships make a team trust you, tell you about problems early, accept change and stay with the organisation. Poor relationships show up as absence, gossip, errors, grievances and staff leaving. In Jamaican workplaces, which are often close-knit and where staff may be friends, relatives or neighbours, the skill is to be warm **and** fair at the same time.
**Who it is for:** team leaders, supervisors and managers in businesses, hotels, schools, public bodies and non-profit organisations.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Act with integrity, keep promises, treat people fairly, protect confidences within limits, and set an example.
Listen actively, give clear feedback, consult staff on decisions that affect them and report back on what was done.
Follow and explain the code of conduct, gifts, conflict-of-interest and social media rules, consistently for everyone.
Identify who you work with inside and outside the organisation and plan how to keep those relationships useful.
Spot early signs, find the cause and the interests behind positions, and use informal, mediated or formal routes.
Hold sensitive conversations, refer to support such as an employee assistance programme, and handle bullying and harassment reports properly.
Use surveys, turnover, absence and grievance figures to judge relationship health and plan improvements.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and short calculations.
A **written paper**: exact terms, quick percentages, and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical group tasks**: a role play resolving a conflict with a written agreement, and a relationship map with an action plan.

blocks.note: In scenario questions, the best answer is usually calm, fair, private, based on facts and within the organisation's policy. Be wary of options that ignore the policy, take sides, gossip, or leave a serious matter alone.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Trust** is the belief that someone is honest, competent and will treat you fairly. It is built by what you do repeatedly, not by what you say once. A new supervisor earns trust fastest by **doing what she says she will do, every time**.

head: Behaviour
How it builds trust
What damages it
rows: You act honestly even when no one is watching and when it costs you
Bending the rules for yourself or for friends
Meetings start on time, promises are kept, deadlines met
Shifts, overtime, leave and praise are shared by clear rules
**Favouritism**: giving better treatment to people you like
You explain decisions and share what you know
You listen, use names, correct in private and praise in public
You admit errors quickly and help to put them right
Blaming others or hiding the mistake

blocks.p: Staff copy what you do, not what you say. A manager who asks for punctuality but arrives late herself will find staff follow her example. Model the behaviour you expect: integrity, respect, fairness, safety and courtesy to customers and colleagues, every day.

blocks.h: When you supervise people who used to be your peers

ul: Meet each person one to one in the first weeks: ask what helps them work well and what they would change.
Say clearly what is changing and what is not.
Apply the same rules to friends as to everyone. If a friend expects special treatment, explain kindly why you cannot give it.
Do not gossip about former colleagues, your manager or other teams.
Ask for feedback after three months and act on it.

blocks.p: **Confidentiality** is the duty to keep private information about staff secure and to share it only with those who need to know. If a team member tells you about a divorce, an illness or money worries, keep it private and discuss support options with her. But you cannot promise absolute secrecy. If she reveals harassment, danger to herself or others, theft or a safety risk, you **must act**, discreetly, and you should say so before she tells you more.

blocks.note: Say: 'I will keep this as private as I can, but if someone is at risk or a rule has been broken, I may have to take it further. I will tell you first.' This is honest and protects both of you.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: In Jamaica, where many staff share a community outside work, be careful that what you hear at work is not repeated at church, at the shop or on the group chat. One broken confidence will cost years of trust.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Rapport** is the trust and easy understanding between two people that lets communication flow. **Active listening** means listening with full attention, summarising what you heard and asking questions to check you understood.

flow: Stop what you are doing and give full attention
Let the person finish without interrupting
Sum up in your own words: 'So the problem is...'
Ask open questions: 'What happened next?'
Agree what will happen and by when

ul: Watch body language, tone and silences as well as words.
Do not start planning your reply while the other person is still talking.
Do not argue or defend while the person is explaining.

blocks.p: A short, regular, private **one-to-one** with each team member (15 to 30 minutes, every two to four weeks) builds rapport, shows you value each person and catches problems early. Agree an agenda: work, progress, development, concerns. Keep brief notes and keep your promises from the last meeting.

head: Part
What to say
Example
rows: What you saw or heard, not what you think of the person
...you said 'not my job' to the customer...
...and the customer left upset. What happened from your side?

blocks.p: Then listen, agree what will change, and follow up. Give feedback soon after the event, in private, about the behaviour, not the person's character. Praise good work in the same way, specifically and sincerely.

blocks.h: Consulting staff on decisions that affect them

blocks.p: **Consultation** means asking for people's views **before** a decision is made, and being ready to change your mind. Staff often know practical problems you cannot see, feel valued, and are more likely to support the result.

flow: Say what the decision is, why it is needed and what is fixed
Choose how to consult (meeting, survey, small groups, one-to-ones)
Give time and listen without defending
Record the ideas and weigh them against cost, rules and goals
Decide and tell staff which ideas were used, which were not, and why
Follow up after the change

blocks.note: Do not consult on something already decided. Fake consultation damages trust more than no consultation. If a decision is fixed, say so and explain it. If only some ideas were used, tell staff which and why.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When new targets, rosters or owner decisions arrive, explain them in a meeting and take questions, then follow up in writing. When rumours spread (for example about job cuts), **share what is known, honestly and promptly**, say what is not known yet and when you will know more. Silence lets rumours grow.

Policies protect people and the organisation, and they make fair treatment possible. A supervisor must know them, explain them and apply them **consistently to everyone**. Staff who see the rules applied the same way trust the supervisor.

head: Policy or document
Purpose
What a supervisor does
rows: Sets the expected behaviour for everyone: honesty, respect, gifts, social media, use of company property
Explains it at induction, models it, deals with breaches under the disciplinary procedure
Declines expensive gifts (such as a weekend trip from a supplier), records small tokens, reports offers
Prevent personal ties affecting work decisions
Declares a link (such as a relative applying for a job in her team) and stays out of the decision
Acts under the conduct and social media policies if a staff member posts insults about a colleague
Fair treatment regardless of sex, age, disability, religion, background and so on
Checks that shifts, training and promotion are decided on clear criteria
Defines unacceptable behaviour and how to complain
Takes every report seriously and follows the procedure
Fair routes for complaints and for misconduct
Follows each step and keeps dated records

blocks.p: Teams include people from rural and urban Jamaica, different ages, faiths, languages and backgrounds, and sometimes staff from other countries. Build relationships by **showing respect and learning about each other**. Do not tolerate jokes or nicknames that demean. Check that a new member is included in lunch breaks, group chats and tasks, and use a **buddy**, an experienced colleague paired with a new team member, to help them settle in.

blocks.h: Handling conflicts of interest and gifts

ul: **Declare** the link or the gift to your manager in writing.
**Step back** from the decision if you have a personal interest.
**Follow the policy** even when you think the gift is harmless: it is the perception and the pattern that matter.
In public bodies, procurement rules and anti-corruption rules apply to gifts and to choosing suppliers.

blocks.p: A manager depends on people outside her team: her own manager, other departments, suppliers, customers, regulators and community groups. A **network** is the group of contacts, inside and outside the organisation, that a manager builds and keeps up for information and support.

A **stakeholder** is anyone affected by, or able to affect, your work. A new operations manager can list everyone her team works with and rate each one's **influence** (power to help or block) and **interest** (how much they care about your work). This tells her where to put her time.

head: Influence
Low interest
High interest
rows: Keep satisfied: brief updates, no surprises
Manage closely: regular meetings, involve in decisions
Keep informed: newsletters, short updates, listen to concerns

head: Relationship
Why it matters
How to keep it healthy
rows: Agree expectations, report problems early with options, raise disagreement privately and with reasons
Meet regularly to agree handovers, such as how orders pass between purchasing and the warehouse
Solve problems fast, better service and prices
Pay on time, be clear and fair, review performance, keep professional distance
Listen to feedback and follow through on promises
Consult early, follow agreements, respect procedures

blocks.p: Disputes between teams, such as purchasing and warehouse arguing over late orders, are best improved by **meeting regularly and agreeing how work is handled**, not by blaming and not by waiting for a crisis.

If you disagree with a decision from above, the professional route is to **raise your concerns privately, with reasons and evidence**, propose an alternative, and then support the final decision in front of your team. Criticising your manager to your team destroys trust in both of you.

blocks.note: Keep network contacts alive in quiet times as well as in a crisis: a short call, a thank-you, sharing useful information. Relationships built only when you need something are weak.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Some disagreement is healthy. **Disagreement about ideas that stays respectful** improves decisions. It becomes a problem when it turns personal, when people stop talking, or when work suffers.

ul: Two people avoiding each other, or sniping and sarcasm
Gossip, cliques, and people leaving a meeting early
Rising errors, delays, absence or complaints
Staff asking to be moved away from someone

head: Cause
Example
Prevention
rows: Two clerks each think the other files the shared records
Two supervisors want the meeting room on Mondays
Sales promise delivery dates the warehouse cannot meet
One person is loud and quick, another quiet and careful
Respect and learning about each other's style
Favoured staff get the best shifts
Everyone overworked in the peak tourist season
Review workloads and rosters with the team

blocks.p: A **position** is what a person says they want ('I need the meeting room every Monday'). An **interest** is the need behind it (she needs a quiet space for weekly calls). Asking 'why?' often finds interests that can be met in more than one way, so both people can be satisfied.

flow: Listen to each person separately, calmly and without taking sides
Check the facts and the policy
Find the real issue and the interests behind positions
Bring them together to agree a solution both can accept
Write down what was agreed, who does what and a date to review
Check in after a few weeks

head: Route
When to use it
Notes
rows: Joint meeting led by the manager
The manager is seen as neutral and the issue is clear
Set ground rules; aim for an agreement both can accept
The dispute has run on, the manager is seen as taking sides, or both are senior
An impartial, trained person helps them talk and find their own solution
Serious matters, or informal routes have failed
Follow the written steps; keep dated notes; each party can be accompanied as the procedure allows

blocks.p: Check in with both people some weeks after an agreement: settled disputes can quietly return. A **grievance** is a formal complaint made by an employee about their treatment at work. If a staff member is unhappy with how her supervisor handled her complaint, she can raise it under the grievance procedure, and the supervisor must not punish her for doing so.

blocks.note: Do not decide who is right at the first conversation. Listen to each side separately first, in private, and check facts. A manager who takes sides early loses the trust of the other person and the team.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Supporting people and handling sensitive matters

blocks.p: Before talking to a long-serving team member whose work has slipped, **gather the facts** (dates, examples, effects) and **plan a private talk**. Start with concern, describe what you have seen, ask for his view, listen, agree actions and a review date. If he mentions money, health or family troubles, offer support.

An **employee assistance programme (EAP)** is a confidential counselling and support service, paid for by the employer, for staff with personal or work problems. A supervisor is **not a counsellor**. Listen kindly, do not diagnose, and refer the person to the EAP, the human resources department, a doctor or other support. Where there is no EAP, know the local services you can recommend.

blocks.note: If someone says they have thoughts of harming themselves, treat it as urgent. Do not leave them alone, stay with them, calmly and without judgement, and get urgent professional help (a doctor, the nearest hospital or emergency services) and inform the right senior person under the policy.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Bullying** is repeated, unreasonable behaviour at work that humiliates, intimidates or undermines a person. **Harassment** is unwanted behaviour (for example sexual, racial or based on a person's disability) that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment. Both can be reported under the organisation's policy, and sexual harassment is also dealt with under Jamaica's law on the subject.

flow: Take the report seriously and thank the person for coming forward
Listen without judging; do not promise secrecy but promise discretion
Write careful, dated notes of what was said
Follow the policy: report to human resources or the designated person
Protect the person from retaliation and, where needed, separate the people during the process
Make sure both sides are heard fairly and the outcome is recorded
Follow up with the person who complained

blocks.p: Dated notes serve a **fair process and an accurate record**. A manager should not investigate alone if the policy gives the task to someone else, should not discuss the case with others, and should never treat a report as a joke or as 'just a personality clash'.

ul: Review workloads and rosters with the team when overwork is harming relationships.
Thank people sincerely and specifically for their effort.
Keep promises about leave and breaks where possible.
Make sure someone who reports a problem is thanked, not blamed.

sections.title: Special situations: change, hybrid teams and new members

blocks.p: Change creates anxiety. Explain **why**, what will and will not change, how it affects each person and where to ask questions. Consult before deciding where you can. Listen to resistance: it often contains real problems. Report back on progress.

blocks.h: Teams that work partly from home

blocks.p: When half of a customer service team works from home, relationships weaken unless you plan for them. Use regular video check-ins, shared team time in the office, clear rules on response times and availability, fair allocation of the best tasks and shifts to remote and office staff alike, and checks that people working at home are not isolated or overworked.

ul: Welcome them on the first day; prepare their desk and access.
Give them a buddy.
Explain the team's rules and ways of working.
Involve them in tasks and social events.
Check in after one week, one month and three months.

blocks.p: Noticing and thanking people sincerely strengthens relationships. Be specific ('Your calm handling of that angry guest saved us a complaint'), prompt, fair across the team, and, where people prefer it, in public. Remember that recognition must be earned and consistent, or it looks like favouritism.

blocks.note: Hotel and tourism teams in Jamaica work hardest in the peak season from December to April. Plan rosters, breaks and recognition so that the pressure does not damage relationships.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: You cannot judge relationship health by feeling alone. Use several sources and look at trends.

head: Source
What it shows
rows: How staff feel about fairness, respect, safety to raise concerns

head: Measure
Formula
Example
rows: Leavers in the year ÷ average staff × 100
Agreement up from 60% to 75% = 15 percentage points

blocks.p: Read figures together. Falling respect scores, rising grievances and rising turnover point to the same problem, so the plan should address the likely causes (for example workload, unfair shift allocation or poor communication) with specific actions, owners and dates.

flow: Gather the figures and feedback
Compare with last year and with other teams
Find the likely causes by talking to staff
Agree a few actions with owners and dates
Carry them out and tell the team
Measure again and review

blocks.p: Ask a trusted colleague and your team for feedback on how you communicate and treat people. Write down what went well, what did not and what you will change. Look for training, a mentor or coaching where you need to improve.

ul: explain how a supervisor earns trust: integrity, reliability, fairness, openness and respect
avoid favouritism and apply rules consistently
keep confidences and explain their limits
listen actively and give feedback using situation, behaviour and impact
consult staff, report back on ideas used, and handle rumours honestly
explain the code of conduct, gifts, conflict-of-interest and social media rules
map stakeholders by influence and interest and plan to keep key relationships healthy
spot the early signs and causes of conflict and separate positions from interests
choose between informal talk, mediation and formal procedures
refer people to an employee assistance programme and respond urgently to risk of self-harm
handle a bullying or harassment report fairly with dated notes
work out percentage agreeing, turnover and percentage change and use them to plan improvements

terms: Trust and easy understanding between two people.
Full attention, summarising and asking questions to check understanding.
A regular private meeting between a manager and one staff member.
Unfair better treatment of people you like.
Keeping private information secure and sharing it only with those who need to know.
Asking for views before a decision is made.
A written list of expected behaviour for all employees.
Anyone affected by or able to affect your work.
Contacts inside and outside the organisation that give information and support.
What a person says they want in a dispute.
An impartial person helps two people reach their own agreement.
A formal complaint by an employee about their treatment at work.
Confidential counselling and support paid for by the employer.
Repeated, unreasonable behaviour that humiliates, intimidates or undermines.
An experienced colleague paired with a new team member.
Leavers in a period as a percentage of average staff.

c1.title: A newly promoted supervisor in a Mandeville accounts office
c1.text: Trevor Campbell has been promoted to lead the accounts team of nine in a Mandeville firm. Three of the team are his close friends. Under the old supervisor, shifts for month-end weekend work were allocated informally and the team's friends usually got the shorter ones. Trevor wants quick trust and a fair team. He is often late for the Monday meeting because of the commute but expects staff to arrive early.

c2.title: A dispute between two dispatchers in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Two dispatchers at a courier depot in Savanna-la-Mar, Dwayne and Keisha, have stopped speaking to each other. Each says the other should update the shared delivery log at 4 p.m., so the log is often incomplete. Dwayne also says, 'I need the late shift every Friday.' When asked why, he explains that he attends evening classes on Thursdays and needs Friday to catch up on rest. The manager, Mrs Edwards, has already supported Keisha in public, and Dwayne now believes she takes sides.

c3.title: Sensitive matters in a Negril hotel's front office
c3.text: Marcia Foster supervises the front office of a Negril hotel. A receptionist, Janelle, tells her that a senior colleague shouts at her and mocks her in front of guests, and has done so for several weeks. Separately, another team member, Omar, who is normally reliable, has become withdrawn and made errors; in a private talk he says he is worried about debts. The hotel has a bullying and harassment policy and a confidential employee assistance programme.

c4.title: Gifts, a relative and key relationships at a Clarendon bottling plant
c4.text: Orville Gray is the purchasing supervisor at a bottling plant in Clarendon. A supplier of packaging offers him a free family weekend at a Negril resort during a contract review. Orville's nephew has applied for a storekeeper job in the warehouse that Orville's team supplies. Orville also wants to improve his relationship with the warehouse team, which often argues with purchasing over late deliveries, and has listed all the people and groups his team deals with, including a public health inspector who has great power over the plant's licence but rarely asks about daily work.

c5.title: Reading the figures for a Portmore call centre
c5.text: A call centre in Portmore averaged 48 staff over the year, and 6 staff left during it. In its staff survey, 40 staff replied each year. Last year 22 of them agreed that 'I can raise concerns safely'; this year 30 agreed. Formal grievances fell from 10 to 7. Since March, 15 of the staff work from home three days a week.

questions.q: What should Trevor do about the month-end weekend shifts?
o: Keep the informal system, because it has worked until now
Give his three friends the shorter shifts to keep them loyal
Set clear, written rules for allocating them and apply them to everyone
Let staff swap freely without telling him
questions.why: Clear rules applied to everyone prevent favouritism, which makes other staff lose trust. Keeping the old unfair system or favouring friends damages his credibility.

questions.q: Trevor is often late for the Monday meeting but expects staff early. What is the likely result?
o: Staff will follow his example, not his words
Staff will respect his busy schedule
Staff will arrive early to impress him
Nothing, because supervisors have different rules
questions.why: People copy what leaders do. Modelling the behaviour he expects, starting with punctuality, is part of building credibility.

questions.q: One of Trevor's friends asks for a favour that breaks the leave rules. What should Trevor do?
o: Grant it quietly, once, as a friend
Refuse without any explanation
Ask the friend to apply through another supervisor
Explain kindly why the rule applies equally to everyone
questions.why: Applying rules consistently, with a respectful explanation, protects fairness and the friendship. Secret exceptions are seen as favouritism and trust falls.

questions.q: Which is the best first step for Trevor in building trust with his new team?
o: Send an email announcing the new rules
Meet each member one to one and listen first
Wait three months before talking to the team
Talk only to the three friends he trusts
questions.why: Individual meetings build rapport and show he values each person's views before he changes anything. Announcing rules without listening, or consulting only friends, risks resentment.

questions.q: Why do Dwayne and Keisha keep arguing about the delivery log?
o: Dwayne is careless with all his paperwork
Roles are unclear about who updates it
Keisha has too little other work to do
The delivery log is kept on paper
questions.why: Each believes the other should do it, so no one is clearly responsible. The root cause is unclear roles, which a written allocation would cure.

questions.q: Dwayne says he needs the late shift every Friday because of his Thursday classes. What has Mrs Edwards found when she asks why?
o: His final position
A grievance
A breach of the code of conduct
His underlying interest
questions.why: 'The late shift on Fridays' is his position. The need behind it, to rest after evening classes, is his interest. Interests can often be met in more than one way, such as a different shift pattern.

questions.q: Mrs Edwards has publicly sided with Keisha, and the dispute has lasted months. What is the best next step?
o: Bring in a neutral, trained mediator
Order both dispatchers to say sorry
Move Dwayne to another depot at once
Wait for it to settle itself
questions.why: Because Dwayne now sees her as biased, an impartial mediator can help both people talk and find their own solution. Forced apologies and transfers do not deal with the cause.

questions.q: What should Mrs Edwards do with the agreement once it is reached?
o: Keep it verbal so that it stays informal
Give a copy to Keisha but not to Dwayne
Write it down, with owners and a review date
Destroy the notes once both have agreed
questions.why: A written, specific agreement owned by both parties, with a review date, prevents misunderstanding. Checking in later shows whether the settlement is lasting.

questions.q: What should Marcia do first about Janelle's report of shouting and mocking?
o: Advise Janelle to ignore it, because the colleague is senior
Ask the colleague privately to tone it down and drop the matter
Take it seriously, make dated notes and follow the policy
Tell the whole team to be kinder
questions.why: A report of repeated humiliation must be taken seriously and handled under the policy. Dated notes give a fair process and an accurate record. Ignoring or privately dismissing it leaves Janelle unprotected.

questions.q: Janelle asks Marcia to promise to tell nobody. What should Marcia say?
o: As private as possible, but she may have to act
That she can promise complete secrecy to Janelle
That she must announce it at the next meeting
That she will tell the senior colleague who it was
questions.why: A manager cannot promise absolute secrecy about bullying or harassment, because the policy requires action. She can promise discretion and to tell Janelle first.

questions.q: In the private talk, Omar mentions debts. What is the most suitable response?
o: Tell him to keep his money problems at home
Discuss his debts with the team to find help
Start the disciplinary process because of his errors
Offer support, such as the assistance programme
questions.why: A supervisor is not a counsellor but should listen, offer confidential support such as the employee assistance programme, and agree a review. Telling him to keep problems home or sharing his private matters breaks trust.

questions.q: What should Marcia do if Omar says that he has thought of harming himself?
o: Tell him to take the rest of the week off
Stay with him and get urgent professional help
Reassure him and wait to see how he is on Monday
Ask a colleague to keep an eye on him next week
questions.why: Risk of self-harm is an emergency. He should not be left alone, and a doctor, hospital or emergency service should be contacted, and the right senior person informed under the policy.

questions.q: What should Orville do about the supplier's offer of a free family weekend?
o: Accept it, because it is during a contract review and not a bribe
Decline it and follow the gifts policy
Accept it, but tell no one
Accept it for his family and pay for his own meals
questions.why: A valuable gift from a supplier during a contract review can influence, or be seen to influence, a purchasing decision. Orville should decline and report the offer under the gifts policy.

questions.q: What should Orville do about his nephew's application?
o: Keep quiet, since the warehouse hires, not purchasing
Rank the nephew's application himself to be fair
Ask the nephew to withdraw his name
Declare the link and stay out of the decision
questions.why: A personal relationship creates a conflict of interest. Declare it in writing and take no part in shortlisting or choosing. Staying silent, or judging his own relative, breaks the rules.

questions.q: Why has Orville listed everyone his team works with and rated each one's influence and interest?
o: To decide where to focus his relationship-building
To make a staff telephone list
To decide who may enter the plant
To work out the cost of each relationship
questions.why: A stakeholder map shows who matters most to the team's work, and how closely each should be managed, so time is used well.

questions.q: On Orville's map, the public health inspector has high influence but low interest in the daily work. How should he treat this stakeholder?
o: Ignore, because the interest is low
Involve in every daily decision
Keep satisfied with brief updates and no surprises
Send a weekly newsletter and nothing else
questions.why: High influence with low interest calls for brief, reliable updates so that the stakeholder is never surprised and stays supportive. Ignoring someone with power over the plant's licence is risky, and heavy involvement wastes both sides' time.

questions.q: What percentage of staff agreed with 'I can raise concerns safely' this year, and what was the change?
o: 30%, up 8 percentage points
75%, up 20 percentage points
85%, up 20 percentage points
questions.why: 30 ÷ 40 = 75% this year and 22 ÷ 40 = 55% last year, so 20 percentage points more. A rise of 36% (8 ÷ 22) is a relative change and is a different measure.

questions.q: What was the call centre's staff turnover rate for the year?
questions.why: Turnover = leavers ÷ average staff × 100 = 6 ÷ 48 × 100 = 12.5%. Using 40 staff gives 15%, which is the wrong base.

questions.q: By what percentage did formal grievances fall?
questions.why: The fall is 10 − 7 = 3. As a share of last year: 3 ÷ 10 × 100 = 30%. Dividing by this year's figure gives 43%, the wrong base.

questions.q: Which action best keeps relationships strong for the staff who work from home three days a week?
o: Ending the home working arrangement at once
Regular video check-ins and shared team time
Contacting them only when there is a problem
Sending written instructions by email only
questions.why: Planned contact and shared team time prevent isolation and weaker rapport. Withdrawing the arrangement or contacting staff only about problems does not build relationships.
